title: Mapping the Formation of Plutonium Oxide via Field Ion Microscopy and Environmental-Atom Probe Tomography
content: Atom Probe Tomography (APT) and Field Ion Microscopy (FIM) are two advanced imaging techniques that rely on field ionization to produce atomically resolved images of materials, with APT producing 3D atom-by-atom composition point cloud maps and FIM producing atomically resolved surface structure maps. When combined, these techniques provide powerful insight into the structure and composition of materials with sub-nanometer spatial resolution and part-per-million mass sensitivity for every isotope in the periodic table. At PNNL, we have made custom modifications [1] to a radiologically capable Local Electrode Atom Probe (LEAP) instrument that allows real-time dynamic imaging of oxidation surface reactions – a mode of APT analysis we call environmental-APT (e-APT) [2]. Here we report the FIM and e-APT analysis of α-Pu to study the dynamics of Pu-oxide formation. Initially, FIM is used to map the atomic surface structure of α-Pu metal so that subsequent localized oxide formation (i.e., corrosion) could be indexed to specific atomic surface features such as various exposed grains or crystallographic pole features. Since α-Pu has a monoclinic crystal structure with a single two-fold rotation axis, no obvious crystallographic pole was observed suggesting, in this case that the specimen was oriented away from the primary axis of symmetry (Fig. 1A-B). The FIM images are produced by field ionization of an inert imaging gas such as Ne or N2, each having a distinct ionization threshold at a given applied field and specimen diameter, from which we can begin to tease out the specific ionization potential of plutonium and plutonium oxide, which is not known. After evaporating the first layers of the Pu specimen, we were able to stabilize the surface and expose three distinguishable nano grains. Following FIM analysis, e-APT is performed with another Pu specimen exhibiting different grains exposed to ∼1×10-9 mbar oxygen at 100 K. Under dynamic field evaporation, the formation of Pu-oxide is observed preferentially over distinct grains. These results are the first of their kind for a Pu material and lay the foundation for understanding the role of surface structures in the dynamic surface oxidation and hydridation reaction studies of Pu metal using e-APT.
